title: Encapsulation
intro: **Encapsulation** means keeping an object's inner details private and offering a clean way to use it. Python relies on naming: a single underscore (`_balance`) means *internal — please don't touch*, and a double underscore (`__secret`) makes Python rename the attribute to discourage outside access. Properties give controlled, validated access.

questions.prompt: A property without a setter is read-only. A setter can validate every change.
questions.explanation: Only `deposit` can change the balance, so the rule is enforced in one place.

questions.prompt: Write `Account(owner)` storing the balance in `_balance` (starting at 0), a **read-only** property `balance`, and `deposit(amount)` that adds to it.

tests.name: deposit
tests.code:
a = Account('Ana')
a.deposit(40)
a.deposit(2)
assert a.balance == 42, 'balance should reflect deposits.'

tests.name: read only

questions.hint: A `@property` with no setter can't be assigned.
questions.explanation: Read-only properties stop outside code changing state directly.

questions.prompt: Double underscores trigger **name mangling**. What does this print?
questions.explanation: It becomes `_A__secret` — hidden, but not truly private.

questions.prompt: Write `Thermostat(target)` with a `target` property whose setter raises `ValueError` unless the value is between 10 and 30. Store it in `_target`.

tests.name: ok
tests.code:
t = Thermostat(20)
t.target = 22.5
assert t.target == 22.5, 'Valid targets should be accepted.'

tests.name: range
init

questions.hint: Assign `self.target` in `__init__` so the setter checks it.
questions.explanation: Validation in the setter covers every way the value can change.

questions.prompt: What does a single leading underscore, like `_cache`, mean?

options.text: It's internal — other code shouldn't use it directly

questions.hint: It's a convention, not a rule Python enforces.
questions.explanation: Other programmers read `_name` as *don't rely on this*.

questions.prompt: Reading `t.temp` crashes with *AttributeError*: the setter stores the value under the wrong name. Fix the setter.

tests.name: value
tests.code:
t = Thermo(18)
t.temp = 21
assert t.temp == 21, 't.temp should be 21.'

questions.hint: The getter reads `self._temp` — does the setter write there?
questions.explanation: The getter and setter must agree on the hidden attribute, `_temp`. (Don't write `self.temp` inside the setter — that calls the setter again forever.)

questions.prompt: Fill in the decorator that adds a setter to the `name` property.
questions.explanation: `@name.setter` attaches the setter to the `name` property.

questions.prompt: Write `Password(text)` that stores only a SHA-256 hash of the text in `_hash` (use `hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()`), never the text itself, and has `check(text)` returning whether the text matches.

tests.name: check
tests.code:
p = Password('correct horse')
assert p.check('correct horse') and not p.check('wrong'), 'check should accept only the original text.'

tests.name: no plain text
tests.code:
p = Password('s3cret!')
assert 's3cret!' not in str(vars(p)), 'The plain password must not be stored anywhere on the object.'

questions.hint: Hash in `__init__`, hash again in `check`, compare.
questions.explanation: Never keep secrets in plain text — even inside your own objects.
Assigning to a property without a setter raises `AttributeError`.

questions.prompt: Write `Inventory` with a private dictionary `_items`. `add(name, qty)` adds stock (`ValueError` if `qty` isn't positive); `remove(name, qty)` takes it away (`ValueError` if there isn't enough). A read-only property `items` returns a **copy** of the dictionary, so outside code can't change the real one.

tests.name: flow
tests.code:
inv = Inventory()
inv.add('pens', 10)
inv.add('pens', 5)
inv.remove('pens', 3)
assert inv.items == {'pens': 12}, 'add and remove should update the stock.'

tests.name: copy
tests.code:
inv = Inventory()
inv.add('tape', 2)
inv.items['tape'] = 999
assert inv.items == {'tape': 2}, 'items should return a copy; changing it must not change the inventory.'

tests.name: rules

questions.explanation: Returning a copy keeps the object in charge of its own data.
